article_title: Hikers lost near Kosciuszko found by artificial intelligence drone
summary: Two hikers lost in Kosciuszko National Park were rescued by an AI-powered drone, marking the first successful use of its AI detection system by Fire and Rescue NSW (FRNSW) for a missing hiker. The drone used thermal imaging and AI detection software to locate the men approximately 500 metres off track. Rescuers then used the drone's built-in speaker to contact the hikers and guide them out, less than five hours after they were reported missing. FRNSW stated the technology significantly reduced search time and risk for rescuers, with plans to improve it for various emergencies.

article_title: Hikers lost near Kosciuszko found by artificial intelligence drone
summary: Two hikers in their early 20s who went missing on the Dead Horse Gap walking track in Kosciuszko National Park were located and rescued by a remote‑controlled drone equipped with artificial‑intelligence detection software. The drone’s thermal imaging and AI analysis identified the men about 500 metres off the trail, and its built‑in speaker allowed rescuers to contact them and guide them out of the park within five hours of the report. This was the first successful use of Fire and Rescue NSW’s AI‑powered drone system, which can recognize humans, vehicles and animals in real time and overlay augmented‑reality maps of fire trails and tracks. FRNSW plans to further develop the technology for broader emergency applications, including delivering overnight care packages to stranded individuals.

article_title: Students protest AI amid growing national concerns
summary: Sunshine Coast Council has partnered with Google and NEXTDC to build the $200 million, five‑storey NEXTDC SC2 AI data centre in Maroochydore, aiming to leverage the city’s proximity to an undersea cable and create a regional digital hub. The project has sparked protests by high‑school and university students, who cite concerns about the centre’s unknown water and energy use, potential environmental impacts, and the effect of AI on future employment. The Greens have called for a moratorium on “hyperscale” data‑centre approvals, while the Council says the facility will be carbon‑neutral and will boost economic growth, connectivity and regional services such as remote health care. University of the Sunshine Coast technology lead Erica Mealy acknowledged the students’ worries but noted that AI can improve lives when applied to hazardous or repetitive tasks.

article_title: Amazon Dropped The OpenAI/Sam Altman Movie. Now Another Distributor Has Picked It Up.
summary: Luca Guadagnino’s biopic “Artificial,” which dramatizes Sam Altman’s 2023 ouster and reinstatement at OpenAI and stars Andrew Garfield as Altman, was abandoned by Amazon MGM Studios after the nearly finished $40 million production. Amazon, which recently pledged a $50 billion partnership with OpenAI, said the film would be “better served” by another studio and put it up for sale. Indie distributor Neon purchased the worldwide rights in a bidding process, declined to reveal the price, and announced a 2024 theatrical release aimed at the Oscar race. The cast also includes Monica Barbaro, Yura Borisov, Mark Rylance and Ike Barinholtz as Elon Musk, and Neon highlighted its strong awards‑season pedigree.

article_title: Three Years After Crippling Strike, SAG-AFTRA Approves New Contract
summary: Television and movie actors overwhelmingly ratified a four-year contract with studios and streaming services on Thursday. Members of the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) approved the deal, which includes protections against synthetic actors created by artificial intelligence. The contract, which is for four years, also provides gains in compensation and reinforces benefit plans. This agreement ensures labor stability and avoids a repeat of the 2023 actor and writer strikes that impacted the entertainment industry.

article_title: Three Years After Crippling Strike, SAG-AFTRA Approves New Contract
summary: The Screen Actors Guild‑American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG‑AFTRA) voted more than 90% of participating members to ratify a four‑year contract with studios and streaming services, securing the agreement that was negotiated a month earlier. The deal includes higher compensation, stronger protections for performers’ digital identities, and provisions that require artificial‑intelligence‑generated actors to add “significant additional value” beyond a live actor or digital capture. Union president Sean Astin said the contract delivers meaningful gains and reinforces long‑term benefit security, while the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers praised the partnership. The agreement mirrors the Writers Guild of America’s four‑year contract and is intended to prevent repeat strikes like those in 2023.

article_title: Stanford was their golden ticket - could AI help or hinder that?
summary: Stanford graduates voiced strong, mixed reactions to artificial intelligence during the recent commencement, with many students walking out of Google CEO Sundar Pichai’s address and displaying signs criticizing Google’s AI ties to ICE and the Israeli military. Interviews revealed a split between optimism—students like computer‑science major Ifdita Hasan see AI as a useful tool for discovery—and concern, as graduates such as Earth‑systems major Atash Heil worry about ethical development, rapid industry transformation, and the environmental impact of data centres. A Federal Reserve Bank of New York analysis and a Stanford study note that early‑career jobs in fields most exposed to AI, including software development, have declined, though most interviewed graduates either have employment lined up or plan further study. Faculty and students also reported changes in academic practices, with increased proctoring to curb “cognitive offloading” and a broader debate about AI’s role in future careers and society.

article_title: 'Green kidneys' of Canberra water catchment fragile to climate change
summary: ACT Parks and Conservation says that climate‑change‑linked impacts are already visible in Namadgi National Park, where the 2020 Orroral Valley bushfire burned about 80 % of the area and sent ash and sediment into the ACT’s water catchment. Rangers are using low‑impact measures—such as shade‑cloth coverings for surviving sphagnum moss and coconut‑fiber “leaky weirs” to slow water flow—to help wetland bogs recover and stay wetter longer. Monitoring data show the mosses are regrowing more quickly and the bogs are retaining moisture, which improves the quality of water that flows to Canberra’s reservoirs. Officials warn that without such interventions the fragile alpine wetlands could disappear as fires become more frequent and temperatures rise, threatening both biodiversity and the city’s water supply.

article_title: NT's new climate resilience plan lists gas project as top priority
summary: The Northern Territory government's new climate resilience plan prioritizes accelerating gas extraction from the Beetaloo Basin. This plan has drawn fierce criticism from environment groups, including the Climate Council, who argue it will increase emissions and worsen climate change. However, NT Environment Minister Joshua Burgoyne states the plan focuses on reducing emissions over time, positioning Beetaloo gas as "low-emissions" to support energy transition. Critics dispute the "low-emissions" claim, highlighting that methane from gas is potent and the plan fails remote communities. The Northern Territory is also noted for being one of the only Australian jurisdictions without legislated emissions reduction targets.

article_title: NT's new climate resilience plan lists gas project as top priority
summary: The Northern Territory’s new climate‑resilience plan lists accelerating gas production from the Beetaloo Basin as a top strategic priority, describing the gas as “low‑emissions” and a means to support long‑term energy security and the national net‑zero‑by‑2050 target. Environment groups, including the Climate Council, the Climate and Health Alliance and the Greens, have condemned the plan, arguing that expanding gas extraction will increase emissions, undermine climate goals and harm public health. NT Environment Minister Joshua Burgoyne said the plan “focuses on reducing emissions over time” and that Beetaloo gas is relatively low in carbon dioxide compared with other Australian gas sources. The plan has drawn criticism for lacking concrete emissions‑reduction targets, with the NT and Western Australia being the only Australian jurisdictions without legislated emissions‑reduction goals.

article_title: Trump Administration Asked National Park Visitors To Report “Negative” History Info. Visitors Did Something Different.
summary: The Trump administration, followed by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, issued an order urging national‑park visitors to report any signs or exhibits that portrayed “negative” aspects of past or present Americans, aiming to emphasize “America’s extraordinary heritage.” An Associated Press analysis of about 35,000 comments submitted between June 2025 and January 2026 showed that more than half were coordinated criticisms of the policy rather than specific flaggings, with many commenters calling the effort “un‑American” or likening it to fascist tactics. A watchdog group, Save Our Signs, documented at least 59 signs that had been removed or altered—covering topics such as slavery, climate change, women’s rights and Native‑American history—most notably at Independence National Historical Park, where exhibits about enslaved people were taken down and later partially restored by court order. The administration has provided little detail on which flagged materials have been changed, stating that many remain unchanged. The comments were released after a Sierra Club lawsuit forced their disclosure.

article_title: Mayors from around world sign pact seeking to rein in data centers
summary: Forty mayors from around the world have signed a new pact to shape the sustainable development and operation of urban data centers. Launched by C40 Cities, an alliance focused on climate change, the pact aims to prevent data centers from negatively impacting cities' natural resources, energy prices, and climate targets. The initiative was driven by concerns from mayors in cities like Phoenix and Melbourne about data centers' high electricity and water consumption, and competition for land. The pact outlines standards for site selection, clean energy use, water reduction, community engagement, and local economic benefits. Mayors hope this unified front will ensure data center investments are beneficial for both developers and local communities.

article_title: Mayors from around world sign pact seeking to rein in data centers
summary: Forty mayors from cities across the United States, Europe, Africa, Asia‑Pacific and the Middle East signed a C40 Cities‑backed pact to set common standards for the siting, energy use, water consumption, emissions and community benefits of urban data centers. The agreement calls for new facilities to be built on abandoned or under‑utilized land, powered by renewable energy and battery storage, to minimize noise, heat and air pollution, and to create local jobs while paying for required infrastructure upgrades. Cities such as Phoenix, which could see its electricity demand double, and Melbourne, where data centers could use up to 4 % of the drinking‑water supply, highlighted the need for the framework to protect residents and climate goals. Southeast Asian cities have not joined the pact, although the region’s data‑center energy demand is projected to more than double in the next five years.

article_title: Prince William arrives by electric bus for climate event
summary: Prince William arrived by electric bus for a climate event in London, where he spoke about the importance of repairing the planet and expressed optimism about the progress of his Earthshot Prize. Marking the halfway point of the 10-year scheme, William highlighted achievements such as cutting 18 million tonnes in emissions and protecting 85 million hectares of land, forests, and rivers. Future initiatives will include improving green energy storage, developing climate-resilient farming, and creating eco-friendly dyes for the fashion industry. London Mayor Sadiq Khan, conservationist Robert Irwin, and Earthshot Prize CEO Jason Knauf also spoke, emphasizing the need for urgency and optimism in tackling environmental challenges.

article_title: Prince William arrives by electric bus for climate event
summary: Prince William arrived at London’s Guildhall by electric bus to address delegates at a climate‑change event during London Climate Action Week, emphasizing the need to “repair” the planet. He highlighted the Earthshot Prize’s mid‑term achievements, noting that award‑winning projects have cut 18 million tonnes of emissions—equivalent to removing four million cars from the road—and protected, restored or improved 85 million hectares of land, forests and rivers. Future prize initiatives will focus on longer‑lasting green‑energy storage, climate‑resilient farming in India, and eco‑friendly dyes for fashion. London mayor Sir Sadiq Khan praised the city’s emissions‑reduction progress and the Prince’s authentic commitment, while speakers stressed the importance of urgency, optimism and scaling successful environmental solutions.

article_title: The UK's summers are getting hotter - but how prepared are we?
summary: The UK is experiencing an unprecedented heatwave, with temperatures in southern England expected to reach 37 °C or higher, surpassing previous June records and following an unusually hot May. Climate scientists say such extremes are consistent with ongoing climate change; the number of days over 30 °C has more than tripled since 2015 compared with the 1961‑1990 average, and six of the last ten years have seen temperatures exceed 35 °C, while projections suggest mid‑40 °C could be possible by 2050. The Climate Change Committee has criticised successive governments for failing to prepare the country’s infrastructure, homes and workplaces for more frequent, severe heat, noting that most homes lack air‑conditioning and that heat can damage railways, roads and increase health risks. It urges urgent investment in cooling technologies, heat‑alert policies and other adaptations, arguing that upfront spending will reduce longer‑term costs and protect public health.

article_title: SA council elections delayed amid review into March poll
summary: South Australia’s parliament passed legislation on 25 June 2026 to postpone local‑government elections for more than 60 councils from 11 November 2026 to 7 April 2027, citing “very serious concerns” from the Electoral Commission about its capacity to run the poll after problems in the March state election. The reform also staggers future council elections to November 2031, 2035 and 2039, separating them from state‑election years in an effort to improve turnout. The bill cleared the upper house with the backing of the Greens and Family First, while the Liberal Party and One Nation opposed the delay. The move follows a request from Acting Electoral Commissioner Leah McLay and an independent review of the March election’s logistical failures. The Electoral Commission welcomed the change as it prepares for the rescheduled vote.

article_title: Acting SA electoral commissioner calls for council election delay
summary: Acting South Australian electoral commissioner Leah McLay has asked Attorney‑General Kyam Maher to postpone the state’s local‑government elections, originally scheduled for November 2026, until mid‑2027. She cites “insufficient” time to implement changes recommended after a review of the March state and First Nations Voice to Parliament elections, which were plagued by staffing shortages, computer glitches, voting‑process confusion and uncounted votes. Maher, who must approve any delay and secure parliamentary approval, said a decision will be made in the coming days, noting that the independent review’s recommendations are expected in September‑October. The delay would affect all 67 councils except Roxby Downs, which is administered, and the Local Government Association is weighing the practical implications.

article_title: Judge halts executive order seeking to create federal voter list...
summary: A federal judge, U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani, issued a summary‑judgment ruling that blocks President Donald Trump’s executive order that would have created a federal “state citizenship list” of eligible voters and limited mail‑ballot delivery to those on the list. The judge held the order unconstitutional because it infringes on the separation of powers, giving the president authority that belongs to states and Congress to set election rules. The decision, brought by a coalition of 22 states, the District of Columbia and voting‑rights groups, applies to the 2026 midterm election cycle and follows a separate recent ruling that blocked another Trump election‑related order. The White House said it will appeal, while state officials praised the ruling as a protection of state‑run elections.

article_title: Key inflation gauge jumps to 3-year high in latest sign of affordability challenges...
summary: The Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, rose 4.1% in May from a year earlier—the largest annual increase since April 2023 and a three‑year high—while monthly inflation was 0.4%, matching April’s gain. The jump was driven primarily by higher gasoline prices, which peaked near $4.50 per gallon, and by rising costs for semiconductors and other computer equipment tied to the AI build‑out, with core PCE (excluding food and energy) climbing to 3.4% year‑over‑year. Despite the higher headline and core rates, consumer spending and inflation‑adjusted incomes each rose 0.3% from April to May, the economy grew at a 2.1% annualized pace in the first quarter, and unemployment claims continued to fall. The data raise concerns that the Fed may need to raise interest rates later this year, a development that could create political challenges for President Donald Trump as the midterm elections approach.

article_title: Trump asks Congress for $87bn, mostly for 'urgent' Iran war costs
summary: The White House has asked Congress to approve $87.6 billion—about $67 billion for the Department of Defense—to fund “urgent needs” tied to the U.S. war on Iran, known as Operation Epic Fury, even though a ceasefire is currently in effect. The request, detailed in a letter from the Office of Management and Budget to House Speaker Mike Johnson, includes $21 billion for munitions, $17.3 billion for operational costs, $12.1 billion for classified programs, $300 million for embassy security, and additional unrelated aid such as $11 billion for farmers and $1.4 billion for Ebola relief. The funding proposal faces opposition after the Senate passed a resolution urging Trump to halt the war or seek congressional approval, a measure supported by a handful of Republicans, including Sen. Bill Cassidy, who later had a tense exchange with the president but changed his vote after receiving a briefing. Analysts note that the Pentagon’s own estimate of the war’s cost—about $29 billion to date—likely understates the total financial impact.

article_title: The Democrats fight back Trump-style in Maine… but have they messed up?
summary: The episode examines the Democratic Party’s decision to run Graham Platner as its Senate candidate in Maine, where he now faces multiple allegations concerning his conduct toward women, which he claims are unfairly amplified. Hosts Justin Webb and North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher discuss voter reactions, the vetting process that led to Platner’s selection, and his upcoming contest against incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins. The program also touches on President Trump’s claims of election fraud in California, the delayed ballot count for the governor’s race, and the candidacies of British‑born Republican Steve Hilton versus Democrat Xavier Baccera. Overall, the discussion explores how these controversies could affect the Democrats’ chances of regaining control of the U.S. Senate.

article_title: Renewables company ZEN Energy enters voluntary administration
summary: ZEN Energy, a South Australian renewable‑energy firm that held a decade‑long contract to supply state‑government sites and was involved in solar‑farm and battery projects, has been placed into voluntary administration after wholesale electricity price volatility undermined its viability. The company’s board cited the volatility as the reason the business could not be sold as a going concern, despite support from the SA Government, SA Power Networks and regulators, and McGrathNicol has been appointed as administrator to assess the business and engage with stakeholders. The state government confirmed that electricity supply to its facilities and essential services has not been interrupted, with former ZEN retail customers now supplied by AGL while a procurement process for a new government‑wide electricity supplier begins. ZEN’s earlier activities included commitments to build a solar farm near Whyalla and a battery near Port Augusta, and its ownership history involved climate expert Ross Garnaut selling the firm to Sanjeev Gupta in 2017 and later reacquiring it.

article_title: Big battery boom means fewer transmission lines will be needed
summary: Australia’s Integrated System Plan shows that 600,000 household batteries and 45 GW of storage projects slated for 2026 are already ahead of the 33 GW target for 2030, easing the need for new transmission lines; AEMO now expects to build about 6,000 km of lines, roughly 1,500 km less than in its previous plan. The report confirms that a renewable‑plus‑gas mix, supported by the expanding battery fleet, remains the cheapest route to the 2050 grid overhaul, which will require $106 billion of private investment, of which $6 billion is for transmission that is projected to save consumers $28 billion. However, wind‑farm approvals are lagging, with only 9 GW of the 18 GW required in the pipeline, threatening the goal of 82 % renewables by 2030. AEMO also flags a rapid rise in data‑centre electricity use—expected to reach about 10 % of total demand by 2050—and the retirement of two‑thirds of the coal fleet by 2035, with none remaining by 2050.

article_title: UKRAINE BOMBARDS RUSSIA
summary: Ukraine carried out a large‑scale nighttime drone raid on a dozen Russian regions, the Russian‑held Crimea peninsula and nearby seas, with Russia’s defence ministry reporting that 660 Ukrainian drones were intercepted – the biggest Ukrainian drone assault since the 2022 invasion, surpassing the previous record of 556 drones on 17 May. Unverified reports said the attacks set fire to a chemical plant and a hydroelectric plant in Novomoskovsk and struck two Russian navy ships and a ferry in the Crimean port of Kerch. The raid followed President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s announcement of a “40‑day influence operation” intended to pressure Moscow to end the war, and came as Ukraine and Russia exchanged 160 prisoners of war. In the same period, Russian strikes killed three civilians and wounded dozens in Ukraine’s Kharkiv, Kyiv, Odesa, Zaporizhzhia and Sumy regions, while Ukrainian air defences downed 174 of 189 Russian drones and intercepted most of the incoming missiles.

article_title: Cuba's iconic antique cars sit idle as US energy blockade deepens fuel crisis...
summary: Cuba’s worsening fuel shortage, which officials attribute to a U.S. energy blockade and tightened sanctions, has left many of the island’s iconic “almendrones” — vintage American cars used as shared taxis — idle. Drivers and owners must wait on a government reservation app, sometimes ranking in the thousands for a 20‑liter allocation, while others turn to a black market where gasoline can cost up to $8 per liter. The scarcity has reduced demand for major repairs and limited the cars’ circulation, even as electric motorcycles, small EVs and solar‑powered charging stations begin to appear. Despite the crisis, some taxi drivers continue to use the classic cars, relying on informal networks to find rides, though tourism and overall demand have sharply declined.

article_title: Oil price falls to levels not seen since before Iran war
summary: Oil prices have fallen to pre‑Iran‑war levels, with Brent crude briefly dipping below $72.48 a barrel—the price on the day before the U.S. and Israel struck Iran on 28 February—before rising to $73.23. The decline follows the June 17 memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Iran, which has led to a gradual reopening of the Strait of Hormuz; about 284 vessels have transited since 18 June, far fewer than the pre‑conflict average of roughly 138 ships per day. Analysts warn that the market remains vulnerable to renewed regional tensions, which could quickly push prices higher again. Lower crude prices are expected to bring UK petrol below 150 pence per litre and diesel under 160 pence within a week, while U.S. gasoline has slipped to about $3.93 per gallon, though it remains above pre‑war levels. U.S. President Donald Trump has ordered an investigation into major energy firms for alleged price‑gouging, despite industry groups noting that fuel prices do not move in lockstep with crude.

article_title: Why hasn't the global economy completely collapsed?
summary: The global economy has avoided a collapse despite the U.S. attack on Iran and the temporary closure of the Strait of Hormuz, with oil prices stabilising around $70 a barrel—still above the pre‑crisis $50‑$60 range. The shock was softened by a pre‑existing global oil surplus (about 3.7 million barrels per day) and large stockpiles, especially in China, which cut its imports by 40 % between February and May. Countries quickly diversified supply: the United States raised crude exports by roughly 25 %, Venezuela and Brazil increased shipments, Singapore began importing U.S. crude, and Gulf producers rerouted oil through pipelines to the Red Sea and Fujairah. The episode also underscored broader trends toward lower energy intensity and diversified energy sources, a shift accelerated after the 2022 Ukraine war, though poorer nations with limited reserves remain vulnerable to price pressures.

article_title: The AI superpower with no seat at the table
summary: Japan and the Philippines have announced bilateral talks to delimit their maritime boundary in waters east of Taiwan, a move that Taipei and Beijing have both protested because it could create enforcement zones that restrict Taiwanese fishing vessels and sideline Taiwan from decisions affecting the area. Beijing responded by launching a “special maritime law enforcement operation” and claiming the waters as part of Chinese jurisdiction, while Taiwan’s President Lai Ching‑te demanded that Taiwan’s rights be respected but used more restrained language than it does toward Beijing. The episode has sparked a domestic political fight in Taiwan, with the opposition Kuomintang accusing the ruling Democratic Progressive Party of double‑standarding China versus Japan and the Philippines and raising broader constitutional questions about Taiwan’s sovereignty. At the same time, KMT chair Cheng Li‑wun’s recent tour of the United States has highlighted the party’s push for cross‑strait economic engagement, contrasting with the DPP’s focus on defensive sovereignty. The dispute illustrates how Taiwan’s strategic and economic importance—exemplified by Nvidia’s new headquarters—can be affected by regional diplomatic negotiations in which it has no seat at the table.

article_title: VEEP MEETS IRAN
summary: High‑level U.S.–Iran negotiations in Switzerland concluded early Monday, after which mediators Pakistan and Qatar said lower‑level technical talks would continue for the rest of the week. The parties agreed to create a “de‑confliction cell” that includes the Lebanese government to monitor and enforce a cease‑fire in Lebanon, while a U.S. team led by Vice President JD Vance met Iranian officials Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf and Abbas Araghchi to discuss Tehran’s nuclear program as part of a 60‑day diplomatic sprint. President Donald Trump’s threatening remarks on social media about Iran’s proxies in Lebanon added tension, but the mediators urged both sides to stay engaged. The emerging agreement also provides temporary sanctions waivers for Iranian oil, outlines mechanisms to keep the Strait of Hormuz open, and contains language on diluting Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile, though Iran maintains its right to continue enrichment.

article_title: The 'King of the North' seeks path to becoming Britain's next leader...
summary: A by‑election in the Makerfield constituency of northwest England on June 18 will decide who fills the vacant Westminster seat, a contest that could position Labour mayor Andy Burnham to challenge Prime Minister Keir Starmer for the party’s leadership and the premiership. Burnham faces Reform UK’s candidate Rob Kenyon, a local plumber whose party is campaigning on a hard‑right, anti‑immigration platform after winning most council seats in the area in recent local elections. The vote comes as Labour’s government struggles with economic, public‑service and immigration pressures, and Starmer’s leadership has been questioned by party members. If Burnham wins the seat, he would gain the parliamentary foothold needed to mount a leadership bid, while a Reform victory would signal a significant shift in a historically Labour stronghold.

article_title: Business Daily
summary: The BBC World Service business program “Taking Stock” (26 June 2026) examined how recent global heatwaves are reducing productivity, increasing energy demand and slowing economic growth. The discussion turned to Germany’s proposed pension‑system reforms and their potential impact on Europe’s largest economy. A dispute over China’s imports of custard apples highlighted rising trade tensions between China and Taiwan. Finally, the panel evaluated whether the week’s sharp swings in technology stocks, including SpaceX, indicate growing investor anxiety about the sector’s outlook.

article_title: Swiss voters set to reject population cap in referendum
summary: Swiss voters rejected the hard‑right “No to a Switzerland with 10 million!” initiative, with early counts showing roughly 55 % voting against the proposal to cap the population at 10 million by 2050. The measure, backed by the Swiss People’s Party, was criticised for threatening the economy and Switzerland’s ties with the EU. In a separate referendum, voters were asked whether to make civilian (conscientious‑objector) service less attractive and accessible; initial projections suggested about 53 % would approve it, though the final result remained uncertain. Both votes were held under Switzerland’s direct‑democracy system on Sunday.

article_title: Why sentiment in Japan has turned against foreigners despite a worker shortage
summary: Anti‑immigration sentiment in Japan has intensified as the far‑right Sanseito party moved from the political fringe to become the fourth‑largest opposition force, winning 15 seats in each house of parliament in 2024 and prompting Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to tighten visa rules, raise foreign‑property requirements and cap the number of foreign residents. A November 2025 Asahi Shimbun telephone poll found 66 % of respondents backed these measures and 56 % said Japan does not need more immigrants, even though the Japan International Cooperation Agency estimates the country will need about 6.7 million foreign workers by 2040 to offset a declining birthrate and shrinking population. Personal accounts, such as those of Nikki Maruschak and her South‑African partner Miguel Carmichael, illustrate a rise in hostile encounters and discrimination against foreigners, while a Stanford Japan Barometer survey showed Japanese preferences favor immigrants from Western nations and those who speak fluent Japanese. Despite the anti‑foreigner mood, Japan continues to pursue tourism growth, targeting 60 million inbound visitors by 2030 and recently raising its international tourist tax to manage overtourism concerns.

article_title: Supreme Court clears way for Trump to revive restrictive immigration policy...
summary: The U.S. Supreme Court voted 6‑3 to overturn a lower‑court order that had blocked “metering,” a practice that limits the number of asylum seekers who can be processed each day at the U.S.–Mexico border. The ruling revives a policy first used under the Obama administration and expanded during President Trump’s first term, though it is not currently being applied and the Department of Homeland Security has not said whether it will be reinstated. In the same decision, the Court also allowed the administration to end a deportation protection for migrants fleeing instability and armed conflict. Justice Sonia Sotomayor dissented, warning that the majority’s opinion undermines the nation’s humanitarian traditions, while Justice Samuel Alito defended the policy as a long‑standing tool for border security.

article_title: By the numbers...
summary: More than 1.17 million immigrants applied for a one‑year, renewable residence permit in Spain’s regular‑status program that ran from April to the end of June, far exceeding the government’s original estimate of 500,000 eligible people. By mid‑June the authorities had processed about 609 000 applications and expected roughly 360 000 applicants to receive temporary work and residence permits, with the final totals to be determined after a three‑month processing period. Approximately 67 % of the applicants were from Central and South America, led by Colombians (26 % of all), followed by Moroccans (13 %), Venezuelans (11 %) and Peruvians (9 %). The measure, described by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez as “an act of justice and a necessity,” marks the sixth mass‑legalization effort in Spain, surpassing the previous record of 576 500 legalizations in 2005.

article_title: David Lammy Tells JD Vance He's Wrong Over Immigration Comments
summary: The episode notes that Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy told U.S. Vice President JD Vance he was “wrong” to blame mass migration for Henry Nowak’s murder during a phone call. Hosts Laura Kuenssberg, Henry and Joe discuss their relationship, why American politicians are focusing on the UK and Europe, and the delay in publishing the government’s Defence Investment Plan. The podcast, produced by Chris Flynn and Maddie Drury with contributions from Joe Wilkinson, Jonny Hall, Chris Gray and Sam Bonham, is available daily on BBC Sounds and can be played on smart speakers. Listeners can contact the show via email (newscast@bbc.co.uk) or WhatsApp (+44 0330 123 9480).

article_title: US Supreme Court upholds birthright citizenship in blow to Trump
summary: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6‑3 that children born on American soil to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present are citizens at birth under the 14th Amendment, rejecting President Trump’s executive order that sought to end the 150‑year‑old birthright‑citizenship policy. Chief Justice John Roberts authored the majority opinion, while Justices Clarence Thomas, Neil Gorsuch and Samuel Alito dissented. The decision is a major setback to Trump’s immigration agenda; Trump said he will pursue legislation to end birthright citizenship, and civil‑rights groups and Democratic leaders praised the ruling.

article_title: WA's Ebola risk is low, chief health officer says
summary: Western Australia’s new chief health officer, Dr Clare Huppatz, said the risk of Ebola entering the state is low because few WA miners travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and the health system has protocols for isolation, triage and contact tracing if a case does appear. She noted that, alongside a Hantavirus‑related cruise ship quarantine and the current flu season, the state is dealing with an unusual diphtheria outbreak in its north, which she believes can be managed through vaccination, antibiotics and contact tracing. Huppatz, who led WA’s COVID‑19 response, warned that another pandemic is possible and that the state is preparing for such threats. As the first woman to hold the role, she hopes to inspire more women to enter public health and plans to focus on improving Aboriginal health outcomes.

article_title: Allegations of double billing and charging for no service at Kalgoorlie hospital
summary: Integral Diagnostics, which runs over 150 radiology clinics in Australia and New Zealand, has been found to bill Medicare for services that are not eligible for bulk‑billing, after an internal memo warned that radiologists were co‑signing referrals to enable such rebates. A similar issue has been raised about its subsidiary Apex Radiology, which provides imaging at the Kalgoorlie Health Campus in Western Australia, where staff were instructed to avoid improper practices such as charging for nonexistent radiologist consultations or double‑billing CT scans. WA Health Minister Meredith Hammat, who previously said there were “no concerns,” has now sought further advice and will refer the matter after being alerted to new information, and the state health department has notified the Commonwealth Department of Health. Both Integral Diagnostics and Apex say they were unaware of any billing errors and will cooperate with any investigations.

article_title: Venezuela digs through quake rubble...
summary: Back‑to‑back magnitude‑7.2 and 7.5 earthquakes devastated Venezuela’s coastal state of La Guaira, leaving at least 920 dead, more than 51,000 missing, over 3,300 injured and only 243 people rescued so far. With few state rescue crews on the ground, residents have taken up shovels and power tools to search the rubble, while authorities have sealed off the epicenter and now require permits for entry. Acting President Delcy Rodríguez has mobilized food, water and military personnel, but the response is described as only a fraction of what is needed. Dozens of international teams—about 861 volunteers and roughly 1,000 responders from 25 countries—are arriving to assist in the search and relief effort.

article_title: COVID-19 vaccine study that was blocked from CDC journal is published elsewhere [Associated Press]
summary: A study of COVID‑19 vaccine effectiveness that had been slated for the CDC’s Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report was blocked by acting CDC director Jay Bhattacharya, who said its “test‑negative” design relied on assumptions that could skew results. The researchers subsequently published the analysis in JAMA Network Open, finding the vaccines were about 55 % effective at preventing COVID‑19‑related hospitalizations and reduced emergency‑department and urgent‑care visits by roughly 50 %. Public‑health experts defended the test‑negative approach as a long‑standing method for real‑time vaccine assessment, while critics—including Bhattacharya and co‑author of the Great Barrington Declaration, Martin Kulldorff—argued it could be biased. A CDC‑hosted forum featured both supporters and detractors of the methodology, underscoring the ongoing debate over how best to measure vaccine performance.

article_title: Starmer and home secretary in row over minister's future
summary: Sir Keir Starmer has refused Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood’s request that immigration minister Mike Tapp be dismissed after he published an unauthorised op‑ed on Home Office policy. Mahmood argued the piece breached collective responsibility and the Ministerial Code, but Downing‑Street said only the prime minister can determine a code breach and that Tapp has been reminded of his obligations. The prime minister’s spokesperson affirmed confidence in both Mahmood and Tapp, while Tapp posted on X that he respects the home secretary and will continue his work. The row stemmed from Tapp’s article defending exemptions for foreign care‑workers in upcoming visa‑rule changes, a component of the government’s broader immigration reforms.

article_title: I take responsibility to fund defence plan extremely seriously, says Burnham
summary: Andy Burnham, the likely new prime minister, told LBC that while he will honour Labour’s manifesto pledge not to raise VAT, income tax or National Insurance, there is “some room” to adjust other taxes. He proposed increasing business rates on large online‑warehouse operators and owners of empty high‑street properties to fund a 20 % rate‑cut for pubs, clubs and music venues and to raise the rate‑paying threshold for small independent retailers for the first time since 2017. Burnham stressed he would not make “crude cuts” to benefits and said any defence‑spending increase announced by Sir Keir Starmer would be funded responsibly, though he has not yet named a chancellor. The interview was his first since announcing his bid for the premiership and he will hold a Reddit “ask me anything” session later in the week.

article_title: Zelenskyy invites Putin to talks to end war in Ukraine
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy published an open letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin proposing a face‑to‑face meeting to negotiate an end to the four‑year war, offering a full ceasefire and an all‑for‑all prisoner exchange as initial steps. He argued that most Russians are weary of missile attacks, inflation and fuel shortages and that both sides are incurring heavy losses, while Ukrainian intelligence warns Russia is planning to extend the conflict into 2027‑28. The Kremlin confirmed it had received the letter; Putin said many questions must be answered before any ceasefire and that a suspension of hostilities is not required to start talks, but Russia would sign peace documents if there is a genuine will to end the war. U.S. President Donald Trump called a meeting “great” and said both parties would need to compromise, and Zelenskyy suggested neutral venues such as Switzerland, Turkey or Arab‑world countries for the talks.

article_title: Time for Russia to make a deal to end Ukraine war, Trump says
summary: G7 leaders at the Évian‑les‑Bains summit agreed to step up pressure on Russia, including new sanctions targeting its gas, oil and LNG‑transport sectors and a broader crackdown on entities linked to Russia’s “shadow fleet.” U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced additional measures against Russian tankers, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney disclosed sanctions on 160 Russian‑related entities. U.S. President Donald Trump, meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Moscow must “make a deal” to end the war, and Zelenskyy reiterated Ukraine’s priorities for more air‑defence missiles, a winter support package and continued pressure on Russia. Macron invited Zelenskyy to remain for the three‑day summit to meet with the G7 heads and discuss the intensified sanctions strategy.

article_title: Putin Faces Crisis as Fuel Shortages Ripple Through Russia...
summary: Ukrainian drone strikes have hit more than 50 Russian oil‑refinery, depot and terminal sites since March, knocking roughly a third of the country’s refining capacity offline and cutting June crude processing by 25% and gasoline output by 17% compared with a year earlier. The damage has triggered fuel‑rationing measures, long queues and price spikes in over half of Russia’s regions, including distant Siberian cities that have not been directly attacked. President Vladimir Putin acknowledged the shortages but described them as temporary and not critical, while analysts say the logistical reallocation of existing stocks will take weeks and that repairs—especially at the Moscow refinery that supplies 40% of the capital’s fuel—will require at least three months. Consequently, the fuel crisis is expected to persist throughout the summer, exacerbated by rising agricultural demand and the difficulty of restoring war‑damaged equipment.

article_title: Russia looks to students to make up for mounting losses in Ukraine
summary: Russia has launched a large‑scale drive to recruit university, technical college and vocational‑school students into “unmanned systems troops,” offering one‑year contracts, high pay (up to five million roubles) and the promise of a safer, high‑tech role as drone operators. The campaign, which began early 2025 and has reached at least 270 institutions, targets young men, especially those struggling academically or facing expulsion, and often pressures them with threats or quotas. Despite the recruitment pitch, drone operators have become high‑value targets; BBC Russian and other sources confirm at least 920 Russian drone operators have been killed since the invasion, a figure likely higher. The deaths of three recent student recruits – Valery Averin, Vladislav Gorbunov and Rakhim Abdullin – illustrate how the promised short, protected service can end in frontline casualties.

article_title: Putin makes rare admission of fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian strikes
summary: President Vladimir Putin publicly acknowledged that Ukraine’s missile and drone attacks on Russian energy infrastructure have created fuel shortages, with queues at petrol stations and restrictions in 56 regions, including a “few days’ supply” left in Crimea. He described the shortage as “not critical” but said Russia will increase air‑defence production, accelerate repairs of damaged refineries and boost fuel deliveries to the peninsula. Putin also claimed the attacks are intended to divide Russian society and weaken support for the war, rejecting Kyiv’s overtures for talks as a tactic to buy time for re‑arming. The Kremlin reiterated its goal of forcing Ukrainian forces out of four southeastern regions it claims as its own.

article_title: SA council elections delayed amid review into March poll
summary: South Australia's local government elections have been delayed until April 2027 after the state government passed new legislation. The delay was prompted by the Electoral Commission raising "very serious concerns" about its ability to administer the poll in November 2026, following issues experienced in the March state election. This change will also ensure subsequent council elections are held in years separate from state polls, a move the local government sector hopes will boost turnout. The legislation passed with support from the Greens and Family First, despite opposition from the Liberal Party and One Nation. Voting for the next council elections will now close on April 7, 2027, instead of November 11, 2026.

article_title: Acting SA electoral commissioner calls for council election delay
summary: South Australia's acting electoral commissioner, Leah McLay, has requested a delay for the upcoming November council elections until mid-2027. This request follows numerous problems during the recent state and First Nations Voice to Parliament elections, including staffing issues, computer glitches, and uncounted votes. McLay believes there is insufficient time to implement recommendations from ongoing reviews before November. Attorney-General Kyam Maher expressed frustration but stated the government would seriously consider the request, noting it would require approval from state parliament. The proposed delay would impact all councils except Roxby Downs.

article_title: Judge halts executive order seeking to create federal voter list...
summary: A federal judge has halted President Donald Trump’s executive order that sought to create a federal voter list and limit who can receive a mail ballot. U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani ruled that the order unconstitutionally violated the separation of powers, stating that states and Congress, not the president, have the authority to set election rules. This ruling applies to the current midterm election cycle. The order was challenged by a coalition of nearly two dozen states, and the Trump administration indicated it would appeal the decision. This marks the second recent legal setback for Trump's election-related executive orders.
